title: Pressure-cooker hard-boiled eggs
subtitle: Easy-peel eggs with consistent results every time
excerpt: Eggs cooked under pressure in steam rather than water. The shells release cleanly, the yolks are fully set, and the method produces consistent results regardless of egg age or variety.
sourceNotes: Pressure-cooking eggs in steam rather than boiling water is a widely documented method in American electric pressure cooker communities. The 5-5-5 method, 5 minutes at pressure, 5 minutes natural release, 5 minutes ice bath, became a standard reference point in the 2010s.

recipe.batchNotes: Cook up to 12 eggs in one batch. Cooking time does not change with quantity.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Hard-boiled eggs keep refrigerated in their shells for up to 7 days.

content.text: Pressure-cooker eggs cook in steam rather than boiling water. Steam penetrates the shell differently to water, so the membrane releases cleanly. The shells peel off easily every time, whether the eggs are fresh or a week old.
The ice bath immediately after cooking is essential. Without it, the eggs continue to cook in their shells from residual heat and the yolks turn grey-green around the edges.
The method works equally for any quantity of eggs, from one to twelve, without adjusting the cooking time. The steam does the work; the number of eggs does not change how long it takes.

Pour 250 ml of water into the pressure cooker. Place the trivet or steamer rack inside, the eggs must sit above the water, not in it. If you do not have a trivet, a tightly crumpled ball of foil works as a stand. Arrange the eggs directly on the trivet.
Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 5 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of exactly 5 minutes, then quick-release any remaining pressure.

Transfer the eggs immediately to a bowl of ice-cold water. Leave for at least 5 minutes. To peel, tap the shell all over on the counter to craze it, then peel under running cold water. The shell should come away in a few large pieces.

rows.symptom: The yolks are grey-green around the edges
rows.cause: The eggs were not transferred to the ice bath quickly enough, or the natural pressure release ran longer than 5 minutes.
rows.fix: The grey-green ring is caused by a reaction between sulphur in the white and iron in the yolk at high temperatures, it is harmless but unpleasant. Move to the ice bath immediately after quick-release, and time the natural release carefully.

rows.symptom: The eggs are difficult to peel
rows.cause: Very fresh eggs tend to be harder to peel in any cooking method. The steam method helps but does not fully overcome very fresh eggs.
rows.fix: Add a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda to the water in the pot, this raises the alkalinity slightly and helps the shell release.

rows.symptom: The yolks are still slightly soft
rows.cause: The natural pressure release was cut short.
rows.fix: Add 1 minute to the pressure cook time next time. For a fully set, dry yolk, cook for 6 minutes at high pressure.

content.text: Hard-boiled eggs are a meal-prep staple. They are protein-rich, portable, and useful across the week in salads, sandwiches, and snacks. The pressure cooker gives a consistent peel every time. No more shells coming off in tiny splinters.
